look_here_first: VASEYGRASS (introduced): first look for a TALL coarse bunchgrass with MANY slender spreading to drooping one-sided racemes along an elongated main axis. Frequently about 10–20 racemes with small 2–3 mm silky-fringed spikelets. Do not confuse with introduced dallisgrass, which generally has fewer (often 3–7) branches and larger spikelets; measured flower parts are key.

crew_field_steps: Trace the single central flowerhead axis and the many narrow racemes spreading in different directions; the installed photo shows this architecture clearly.
Recognize that each slender raceme carries rows of tiny spikelets along one side; the individual hairs are not resolvable in the wide view.
Collect base/ligule, a measured spikelet and the FULL head to distinguish dallisgrass; a distant photograph alone is only a vaseygrass candidate.
what_to_photograph_for_confirmation: Whole rooted bunch, height context, basal sheaths.
One ENTIRE panicle with every raceme attachment visible.
Macro of pairwise spikelets next to millimeter scale and silky margin hairs.
True membranous ligule at blade/sheath junction; compare dallisgrass.

comparisons.key_distinctions: Vaseygrass tends to be taller with more racemes (commonly 10–20) and small roughly 2–3 mm hairy spikelets; dallisgrass usually bears fewer racemes and bigger 3–4 mm silky-edged spikelets. Florida paspalum generally has fewer racemes and large broad spikelets. Johnson grass has an open branching PANICLE rather than the flat, one-sided raceme rows typical of Paspalum.
